The grand dining room of the Hôtel des Eaux Vives was a cavern of heavy velvet and polished brass, its low hum a comfortable lullaby to the weary guests. The scent of truffle-infused oil and roasted duck filled the air, rich and decadent. At the centre of the table was Madame Élise Laurent, a formidable woman whose reputation in the finance world commanded a deference that bordered on fear. Around her sat five others: her business partner, a nervous-looking accountant; a haughty banker from Zurich; a quiet young journalist; a distant English diplomat; and Élise herself, eating slowly, her eyes sharp as she divined the motives of everyone at the table.

The waiter, a man named Henri, moved through the room with the practiced grace of someone who had served these same faces a hundred times. He carried a tray laden with a final course—crème brûlée—and approached Élise’s place. He presented the dish with a small, precise bow, the gesture almost too fluid, too perfectly choreographed. There was something unnervingly smooth about the way he moved, the way his eyes flickered towards her with an intensity that wasn’t quite professional.

Élise smiled graciously and accepted the bowl. She broke through the caramelised sugar with her spoon, the sound delicate on the hushed evening. She took a small bite.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then, her brow furrowed. It was the slightest flicker of annoyance, a momentary grimace as if something had simply been slightly off in flavour. “Henri,” she said, her voice still polite but edged with a new note of demand. “The custard seems a fraction too… runny? It lacks the body it had earlier at the staff dinner.”

Henri’s expression did not change. “Ma’moiselle Laurent. It is precisely the same recipe. Perhaps the temperature of your room has affected your palate?” His voice was perfectly clear, lacking any inflection that might betray guilt or amusement.

Élise pushed the bowl away slightly, a gesture so small it could have been a momentary loss of balance. “No,” she said, a single word that dropped into the silence like a stone. “No, I am certain.” She wiped her mouth with the napkin, her movements becoming economical and guarded. The polite dinner conversation, once a steady stream, faltered. The banker muttered something about late trains; the journalist stopped scribbling. A silence descended that was heavier than anything the room had known.

Unnoticed by everyone, Detective Marc Reus leaned back in his chair at the far end of the table, hidden in the deep shadow of a tapestry. He had been observing the room with half-lidded eyes, letting the tension build without drawing attention. But Élise’s reaction was a key turning point. He watched as Henri, instead of simply apologising and bowing out, lingered a second too long at the edge of Élise’s field of vision, his posture subtly shifting to stand just where he could watch her spoon make another pass over the dessert.

While the guests exchanged uneasy smiles and diverted their attention back to their wine, the detective’s gaze sharpened. He didn’t see chemistry; he saw intent. He saw the way Henri kept his hands visible, his palms open and empty, yet his eyes rarely left Élise’s mouth. It was a dance of distraction.

And then it happened.

Élise touched her lips with the back of her hand. A barely-there flick of the wrist. An involuntary rubbing, as if a stray hair had irritated her or a sudden itch had appeared. It was subtle, almost imperceptible to anyone but one watching closely for it. But to Marc, it was the crack in the dam. She had felt something unpleasant, not just tasted it.

The murmurs resumed, louder now to mask the growing unease. But Marc Reus lifted his glass, his expression bland. He took one sip, then set it down slowly. He didn’t look at the food; he looked at the hands. Henri’s hands were still pale and steady. Yet, on the cuff of his pristine white jacket, a tiny, almost invisible smear of something yellowish-white was beginning to show through the fabric. It wasn’t soup or sauce. It was dry. It was crystalline.

Marc didn’t gasp. He didn’t point. He simply adjusted his collar slightly, his gaze sliding away to the dessert cart in the corner, where the silver was polished to a mirror sheen.

The play was over, but the curtain had not yet risen. And somewhere in the dark, behind the eyes of a seemingly devoted waiter, the first act of murder had already succeeded.
